The Story of Dipayan Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the lord of the world and bestower of infinite happiness, and I write the story of Dipayan Muni, as recorded by the ancient teachers.

In the land of Sorath stands the famous city of Dwaraka, where Lord Neminath was born, making it a sacred place. At the time of this story, the ninth Narayan Balbhadra and Vasudev ruled Dwaraka. One day, both these great kings went to Girnar Mountain to worship Lord Neminath. They worshipped the Lord with devotion and heard his discourse. The teaching pleased them greatly. Afterward, Balbhadra asked the Lord, "O causeless binder of the world, O holder of the eye of omniscience, O lord of the three worlds, O ocean of compassion, O illuminator of the world and beyond — please tell us, how long will the wealth that Vasudev has through merit remain?"

The Lord replied, "It will remain with Vasudev for twelve years and then be destroyed. Moreover, the entire Yadu clan will be destroyed by drinking alcohol. Dwaraka will be burned to ashes in connection with Dipayan Muni. And Balbhadra, you will be the cause of Shrikrishna's death through this knife, at the hands of Jaratkumar."

Hearing the Lord's prophecy about the Yadu clan, Dwaraka, and Vasudev, Balbhadra returned to Dwaraka. He had all the alcohol in the city poured into the forests of Girnar Mountain. Dipayan, upon hearing that Dwaraka would be destroyed because of him, became a monk and left Dwaraka for another place. Fools may try to prevent destiny, but the Lord's word is never false.

As for the knife — Balbhadra had it ground down to nothing and thrown into the ocean. But through the workings of karma, a fish swallowed the remaining blade, and that fish was caught in a fisherman's net. The knife was found in its belly and eventually reached the hands of Jaratkumar, who fashioned it into an arrowhead.

Twelve years passed — or so Dipayan thought, though it had actually been more than twelve years. He returned toward Dwaraka and stayed near Girnar Mountain, practising austerity. Meanwhile, the Yadu clan, having drunk the alcohol that had seeped into the plants and water, fell into drunken quarrels and destroyed each other. Dwaraka was consumed by fire. And Shrikrishna, wandering in the forest, was killed by Jaratkumar's arrow — the very arrow tipped with the knife Balbhadra had thought destroyed.

This story teaches that the word of the omniscient Lord can never be in vain. No matter how hard Balbhadra tried to prevent the prophecy, every detail came to pass exactly as foretold. The wise should understand that karma is inexorable, and the predictions of the all-knowing are certain. One should therefore follow the path of dharma and not try to fight against the inevitable fruits of one's actions.
